The Turquoise killifish Nothobranchius furzeri is an annual fish species inhabiting seasonal water bodies in southeastern Africa, where rapid development is essential for population persistence. Embryonic development proceeds within diapausing eggs that remain buried in dry sediment, and when inundated at a water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], hatching occurs after an incubation period of 20 days [ab = 20 days]. Upon emergence from the chorion, the newly hatched larvae measure approximately 0.46 cm [Lb = approximately 0.46 cm] in total length from snout to caudal fin tip and possess a minuscule body mass of 0.000905 g [Wwb = 0.000905 g], reflecting the small size of the yolk-laden egg from which they hatch. This extraordinarily low neonatal mass places the species among the smallest teleost hatchlings documented for its body size range, an adaptation linked to the ephemeral nature of its temporary pool habitat where early and rapid growth confers a selective advantage.

As the young larvae initiate exogenous feeding, they enter a phase of accelerated somatic growth that is highly temperature-dependent. Sexual maturation, defined by the onset of gonadal recrudescence and gametogenesis, occurs remarkably quickly under optimal thermal regimes. When larvae are reared at a constant temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C], individuals attain puberty approximately 13 days after emergence from the egg [tp = approximately 13 days after emergence from the egg]. By this point, the juveniles have reached a total length of roughly 2.5 cm [Lp = roughly 2.5 cm], a size threshold that coincides with the differentiation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and the initiation of vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males. This extraordinarily compressed developmental schedule, completing sexual maturation in under two weeks, is among the fastest recorded for any vertebrate species and is directly tied to the selective pressures of an unpredictable arid environment.

Growth continues rapidly after puberty, with males and females diverging in their ultimate body dimensions, a pattern typical of many killifish species that exhibit pronounced sexual size dimorphism. Adult females attain a maximum total length of approximately 4.9 cm [Li = approximately 4.9 cm], with a corresponding wet body mass of around 0.55 g [Wwi = around 0.55 g], while males grow substantially larger, reaching an ultimate total length of about 6.8 cm [Li = about 6.8 cm] and achieving a wet weight of 1.54 g [Wwi = 1.54 g]. This size dimorphism is thought to be driven by intrasexual selection, as larger males are more successful in competing for access to gravid females in the shallow, confined pools they inhabit. The asymptotic mass and length values appear to be constrained by the finite resources available within the ephemeral habitat, with individuals rarely exceeding these reported maxima even under optimal captive conditions.

Reproductive output in Nothobranchius furzeri is characterized by a high investment in individual offspring quality, consistent with a strategy of producing relatively few, large eggs that are resistant to desiccation. Females lay between 5 and 15 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = between 5 and 15 eggs per spawning event], and under the warm, stable conditions of the laboratory, they may spawn daily, achieving a frequency of approximately one clutch per day [F_R_i = approximately one clutch per day]. The eggs, each measuring about 1.2 mm in diameter, are deposited singly into the substrate, where they enter a developmental arrest phase. This iteroparous spawning pattern, combined with daily egg deposition, allows females to distribute reproductive effort across the entire adult lifespan, maximizing the probability that at least some offspring will encounter favorable conditions for hatching in the unpredictable seasonal environment.

One of the most striking features of the Turquoise killifish is its compressed lifespan. When maintained at a constant temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the maximum documented longevity for this species is 112 days [am = 112 days], a remarkably short duration that classifies it as one of the shortest-lived vertebrates known to science. This rapid senescence is associated with a suite of physiological changes, including progressive deterioration of organ function and the accumulation of cellular damage, that ultimately lead to organismal death following the completion of the reproductive period. Interestingly, lifespan can be extended by reducing water temperature, suggesting that the rate of aging is metabolically modulated and that the species serves as a valuable model organism for studies of accelerated senescence and age-related pathologies in a natural ecological context.
